quote: I realize now that when I wrote “You cannot make yourself believe the sky is green by an act of will,” I wasn’t just a dispassionate reporter of the existing facts. I was also trying to instill a self-fulfilling prophecy.
content: The essay discloses its own move, in public, in the sequence, which is the behaviour the annotations elsewhere say the book fails to exhibit. And the thing disclosed is not a false belief chosen for its benefits: the claim "you cannot make yourself believe the sky is green by an act of will" is one the essay still holds to be true, and the admission is that it was also stated emphatically because emphasis has effects. Choosing which true things to say forcefully is not belief in belief; the Litany of Tarski governs what you believe, not what you stress.

quote: Shouldn’t the gut-level realization, “Oh, wait, the sky really isn’t green” follow from the realization “My map that says ‘the sky is green’ has no reason to be correlated with the territory”?
content: The continued-influence effect is the essay's finding, not a rebuttal of it, and the essay is the one reporting it: knowing a belief's origin does not remove the belief. What the annotation reads as an admission that the book's method fails is the book applying its method and getting an honest negative result, which is how the sequence's later essays on debiasing proceed. The remedy the essay reaches for is not "a chant" but a policy adopted in advance, before the situation arises, which is the structural rather than introspective approach the annotations elsewhere recommend.
